column1: 1706.03762|Attention Is All You Need|Transformers|Self-attention lets every token combine information from other tokens. Multi-head attention learns different relationships; positional encodings supply order. Compare attention cost with recurrent models.

1810.04805|BERT|Transformers|Masked language modelling learns bidirectional representations. Fine-tuning adapts the encoder to downstream tasks. Contrast masked-token training with autoregressive next-token prediction.

2005.14165|Language Models are Few-Shot Learners (GPT-3)|Transformers|Scaling autoregressive language models enables in-context task demonstrations. Few-shot prompting changes the context without updating weights. Distinguish in-context learning from fine-tuning.

1910.10683|Exploring the Limits of Transfer Learning (T5)|Transformers|A unified text-to-text format expresses many NLP tasks with one interface. The paper compares pretraining choices and transfer settings. Study span corruption and encoder-decoder generation.

1907.11692|RoBERTa|Transformers|Training choices substantially affect BERT performance. More data, longer training and dynamic masking improve the recipe. An architectural change is not always needed for a stronger baseline.

1906.08237|XLNet|Transformers|Permutation language modelling combines autoregressive objectives with access to varied context orders. Two-stream attention avoids leaking the prediction target. Compare its objective with BERT masking.

1909.11942|ALBERT|Transformers|Factorised embeddings and cross-layer parameter sharing reduce parameter count. Sentence-order prediction supplies a pretraining signal. Parameter savings do not automatically imply proportional compute savings.

1910.13461|BART|Transformers|A bidirectional encoder and autoregressive decoder reconstruct corrupted text. Denoising pretraining supports generation tasks. Compare reconstruction with T5 span corruption.

2001.04451|Reformer|Transformers|Locality-sensitive hashing approximates attention and reversible layers reduce activation memory. Efficiency comes with approximation and implementation trade-offs. Separate memory complexity from wall-clock speed.

2004.05150|Longformer|Transformers|Local sliding-window attention combines with selected global attention positions. This enables longer documents without full quadratic attention. Global-token choice matters for the task.

2009.14794|Performer|Transformers|Random-feature approximations estimate softmax attention with linear scaling. Approximation quality depends on feature construction and count. Compare approximate attention with exact kernel optimisations.

2006.04768|Linformer|Transformers|Low-rank projections compress the sequence dimension of keys and values. The method reduces attention complexity under a low-rank hypothesis. Ask how sequence length and projection rank affect fidelity.

2205.14135|FlashAttention|Transformers|Tiling and online softmax reduce memory traffic for exact attention. The central insight is hardware-aware IO efficiency. It does not replace exact attention with a sparse approximation.

2307.08691|FlashAttention-2|Transformers|Improved work partitioning and parallelism increase attention throughput. The method retains exact attention while changing GPU execution. Hardware utilisation matters alongside asymptotic complexity.

2104.09864|RoFormer|Transformers|Rotary position embeddings rotate query and key vectors to encode positions. Their dot products incorporate relative positional structure. Separate position representation from attention sparsity.

2108.12409|Train Short, Test Long (ALiBi)|Transformers|Attention logits receive head-specific linear distance biases. This avoids learned positional embeddings and studies length extrapolation. Extrapolation performance is an empirical question.

1901.02860|Transformer-XL|Transformers|Segment-level recurrence reuses previous hidden states. Relative positional encodings help maintain temporal consistency across segments. Reused states extend context without backpropagating through all history.

2001.08361|Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models|Scaling|Model size, data and compute exhibit empirical power-law relationships with loss. Compute allocation becomes a design problem. These fitted laws describe specific training regimes rather than universal guarantees.

2203.15556|Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models (Chinchilla)|Scaling|Jointly scaling training data and parameters changes compute-optimal model design. The work challenges recipes with large models trained on too few tokens. Compare a fixed compute budget across configurations.

2204.02311|PaLM|Scaling|Large-scale dense language modelling studies scaling across many tasks. Architecture and distributed training choices support the model. Examine multilingual performance and evaluation limitations separately.

2302.13971|LLaMA|Scaling|Training open foundation models on public data emphasises inference-efficient model sizes. More training tokens can improve smaller models. Compare training cost with deployment cost.

2307.09288|Llama 2|Scaling|Pretraining and dialogue alignment produce a family of language models. Supervised tuning and preference optimisation shape chat behaviour. Separate base-model capability from alignment effects.

2310.06825|Mistral 7B|Scaling|Grouped-query and sliding-window attention support efficient inference. Model quality depends on both training and architecture. Inspect which attention mechanisms are actually used in a checkpoint.

2401.04088|Mixtral of Experts|Scaling|Sparse expert routing activates only a subset of feed-forward networks per token. Total parameters differ from active parameters. Routing, memory and communication affect practical efficiency.

2101.03961|Switch Transformers|Scaling|Simplified sparse routing scales model capacity while limiting per-token computation. Load balancing and training stability are central challenges. Compare dense compute with expert capacity.

1701.06538|Outrageously Large Neural Networks (MoE)|Scaling|A sparsely gated mixture-of-experts layer routes examples to selected experts. Conditional computation increases capacity without activating all weights. Load imbalance can erase theoretical efficiency gains.

2106.09685|LoRA|Adaptation|Low-rank matrices represent weight updates while pretrained weights remain frozen. Training fewer parameters reduces optimiser memory. Distinguish low-rank adaptation from low-rank compression of the base model.

2305.14314|QLoRA|Adaptation|Quantisation of frozen base weights combines with low-rank adapters. Quantisation-aware storage and paged optimisers reduce fine-tuning memory. Check training memory separately from inference performance.

1902.00751|Parameter-Efficient Transfer Learning for NLP (Adapters)|Adaptation|Small trainable modules adapt a frozen pretrained model. Task-specific parameters are stored separately. Compare adapter placement with LoRA weight updates.

2101.00190|Prefix-Tuning|Adaptation|Trainable continuous prefixes steer a frozen model. The learned prefix differs from a human-written text prompt. Compare prefix length, task performance and trainable parameter count.

2104.08691|The Power of Scale for Parameter-Efficient Prompt Tuning|Adaptation|Soft prompt embeddings adapt frozen language models. Their effectiveness changes with model scale. Prompt tuning and full fine-tuning have different storage and training costs.

2106.10199|BitFit|Adaptation|Updating only bias terms can provide a parameter-efficient adaptation baseline. Its strength varies by task and data regime. Simple baselines help test whether a more complex method is needed.

2402.09353|DoRA|Adaptation|Weight decomposition separates magnitude from direction during adaptation. Low-rank updates operate on direction with additional magnitude learning. Compare gains against LoRA under matched budgets.

1707.06347|Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO)|Reinforcement learning|A clipped surrogate objective discourages excessively large policy updates. On-policy samples estimate policy gradients and advantages. Clipping is a practical stabiliser, not a strict trust-region guarantee.

1502.05477|Trust Region Policy Optimization (TRPO)|Reinforcement learning|Policy improvement is constrained using a KL-divergence trust region. Approximate optimisation makes the update tractable. Compare the explicit constraint with PPO clipping.

1312.5602|Playing Atari with Deep Reinforcement Learning (DQN)|Reinforcement learning|A neural network estimates action values from pixels. Experience replay reduces correlations in training samples. Distinguish value-based control from direct policy optimisation.

1509.02971|Continuous Control with Deep Reinforcement Learning (DDPG)|Reinforcement learning|An actor-critic method combines deterministic policy gradients and replay. Target networks support more stable learning. Continuous actions require a different maximisation strategy from discrete DQN.

1801.01290|Soft Actor-Critic|Reinforcement learning|Maximum-entropy reinforcement learning rewards both return and policy entropy. Off-policy training reuses experience. The entropy coefficient controls an exploration-performance trade-off.

1802.09477|Addressing Function Approximation Error in Actor-Critic Methods (TD3)|Reinforcement learning|Twin critics, delayed policy updates and target smoothing reduce overestimation problems. Critic error can propagate into poor policies. Compare these mechanisms individually through ablations.

1506.02438|Generalized Advantage Estimation|Reinforcement learning|Exponentially weighted temporal-difference residuals estimate advantages. A lambda parameter trades bias against variance. Advantage estimation is distinct from the policy-update objective.

1602.01783|Asynchronous Methods for Deep Reinforcement Learning (A3C)|Reinforcement learning|Parallel actor-learners decorrelate experience and update a shared model. Actor-critic training combines policy and value learning. Compare asynchronous sampling with replay-based approaches.

1710.02298|Rainbow|Reinforcement learning|Several DQN improvements are combined and studied through ablations. Distributional learning, prioritisation and multi-step returns address different issues. Combined performance does not identify each component's contribution.

1707.01495|Hindsight Experience Replay|Reinforcement learning|Failed goal-conditioned trajectories can be relabelled with achieved goals. Sparse rewards become more informative. Relabelling depends on a compatible goal and reward formulation.

2106.01345|Decision Transformer|Reinforcement learning|Offline reinforcement learning is formulated as sequence modelling conditioned on desired return. A causal transformer predicts actions from trajectories. Dataset coverage constrains what the learned policy can do.

1706.03741|Deep Reinforcement Learning from Human Preferences|Alignment|Pairwise human comparisons train a reward model for policy learning. Preference labels replace direct reward engineering. Reward-model errors can be amplified by optimisation.

2203.02155|Training Language Models to Follow Instructions (InstructGPT)|Alignment|Supervised demonstrations and human preferences align language-model outputs. A learned reward model guides policy optimisation. Helpfulness and truthfulness require separate evaluation.

2305.18290|Direct Preference Optimization (DPO)|Alignment|A preference objective directly updates a language model relative to a reference policy. The formulation avoids an explicit online RL loop. Preference data quality and reference choice still matter.

2212.08073|Constitutional AI|Alignment|Written principles guide critique, revision and preference-based alignment. AI feedback can reduce some human labelling needs. The chosen principles encode normative assumptions.

2009.01325|Learning to Summarize from Human Feedback|Alignment|Human comparisons train reward models for summarisation. Optimising preference reward can improve judged quality. Evaluate factuality separately from preference scores.

2201.11903|Chain-of-Thought Prompting|Reasoning|Worked intermediate reasoning examples can improve performance on multi-step tasks. The method changes the prompt without updating model weights. A plausible explanation is not proof of correct reasoning.

2203.11171|Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning|Reasoning|Multiple sampled reasoning paths vote on a final answer. Diversity can improve reliability at additional inference cost. Agreement can still preserve shared mistakes.

2205.11916|Large Language Models are Zero-Shot Reasoners|Reasoning|A simple reasoning cue can elicit intermediate steps without worked demonstrations. Performance depends on model and task. Check answers rather than trusting fluent steps.
2210.03629|ReAct|Reasoning|Language-model reasoning interleaves with actions and observations. External tools supply evidence and state changes. Tool outputs must be validated and treated as data.

2305.10601|Tree of Thoughts|Reasoning|Search explores and evaluates multiple intermediate reasoning states. Branching and backtracking extend linear chain-of-thought prompting. Better results can require substantially more inference.

2302.04761|Toolformer|Reasoning|A language model learns when and how to call tools from generated examples. Tool use is incorporated into language-model training. Separate tool-call correctness from final-answer quality.

2303.11366|Reflexion|Reasoning|Verbal feedback is stored to improve later attempts. This resembles an external memory loop rather than gradient-based learning. Feedback quality limits iterative improvement.

2005.11401|Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks|Retrieval|A retriever supplies passages to a generator. Retrieval allows external knowledge to support answers without storing everything in parameters. Evaluate retrieval recall and grounded generation separately.

2004.04906|Dense Passage Retrieval|Retrieval|Dual encoders map questions and passages into a shared vector space. Inner-product search retrieves relevant passages. Negative-sampling choices influence retrieval quality.

2004.12832|ColBERT|Retrieval|Token-level embeddings support late interaction between queries and documents. This retains finer matching than a single vector per document. Index size and query latency are key trade-offs.

2112.04426|Improving Language Models by Retrieving from Trillions of Tokens (RETRO)|Retrieval|Retrieved text chunks condition language modelling during training and inference. External memory changes the relationship between parameters and knowledge. Consider corpus contamination and retrieval cost.

2212.10496|Precise Zero-Shot Dense Retrieval without Relevance Labels (HyDE)|Retrieval|A generated hypothetical document becomes the query representation for dense retrieval. The generated text is a search aid, not verified evidence. Retrieved sources must still support the answer.

2310.11511|Self-RAG|Retrieval|Reflection tokens help a model decide when to retrieve and assess support. Retrieval and generation are coordinated through training. Citation presence alone does not establish citation correctness.

2404.16130|From Local to Global: A Graph RAG Approach|Retrieval|Entity relationships and hierarchical community summaries support global corpus questions. Graph construction adds a preprocessing stage. Compare local fact lookup with corpus-wide thematic synthesis.

1911.00172|Generalization through Memorization: Nearest Neighbor Language Models|Retrieval|Nearest-neighbour retrieval over a datastore augments language-model predictions. Nonparametric memory can adapt knowledge without retraining all weights. Datastore construction influences cost and relevance.

1406.2661|Generative Adversarial Nets|Generative models|A generator and discriminator learn through an adversarial objective. The generator tries to match the data distribution. Training instability and mode collapse motivate later variants.

1312.6114|Auto-Encoding Variational Bayes (VAE)|Generative models|A variational bound trains a probabilistic latent-variable model. The reparameterisation trick enables gradient estimates. Reconstruction and latent regularisation pull in different directions.

1511.06434|Unsupervised Representation Learning with DCGANs|Generative models|Convolutional architectural choices improve adversarial image modelling. Learned features can transfer to other tasks. Architecture and optimisation choices influence GAN stability.

1701.07875|Wasserstein GAN|Generative models|An alternative distribution distance supplies a critic-based training objective. A Lipschitz constraint is central to the formulation. The original weight-clipping implementation has limitations.

1704.00028|Improved Training of Wasserstein GANs|Generative models|A gradient penalty replaces weight clipping to constrain the critic. This can improve training behaviour. The penalty is applied on sampled interpolations rather than everywhere.

1812.04948|A Style-Based Generator Architecture for GANs (StyleGAN)|Generative models|A mapping network and layer-wise style controls separate aspects of image generation. Noise models stochastic details. Latent controls are not guaranteed to be perfectly disentangled.

2006.11239|Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models|Generative models|A forward noise process is reversed by learned denoising steps. The training objective connects to denoising score matching. Sampling quality and sampling cost must be considered together.

2010.02502|Denoising Diffusion Implicit Models|Generative models|Alternative reverse processes reuse a diffusion training objective. Deterministic sampling paths can reduce the number of generation steps. Fewer steps can change quality.

2011.13456|Score-Based Generative Modeling through Stochastic Differential Equations|Generative models|Stochastic differential equations unify continuous-time diffusion and score models. Reverse dynamics use learned scores. Numerical solvers affect generation speed and quality.

2112.10752|High-Resolution Image Synthesis with Latent Diffusion Models|Generative models|Diffusion operates in a learned latent space instead of raw pixels. Cross-attention supports conditioning. Autoencoder reconstruction sets a practical limit on preserved detail.

2207.12598|Classifier-Free Diffusion Guidance|Generative models|Conditional and unconditional predictions are combined during sampling. Guidance strength trades diversity against prompt adherence. Larger guidance is not uniformly better.

2212.09748|Scalable Diffusion Models with Transformers (DiT)|Generative models|Transformer backbones replace common convolutional diffusion architectures. Patchified latent inputs enable scaling experiments. Compare compute budgets as well as parameter counts.

1503.03585|Deep Unsupervised Learning using Nonequilibrium Thermodynamics|Generative models|A gradual noising process is paired with a learned reverse process. This early diffusion formulation motivates later denoising models. Study the connection between transitions and likelihood bounds.

1512.03385|Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition (ResNet)|Vision|Skip connections let layers learn residual functions. They ease optimisation of very deep networks. Residual connections differ from simply adding more layers.

1409.1556|Very Deep Convolutional Networks (VGG)|Vision|Stacks of small convolutions build deep image representations. Depth and regular architecture are the central ideas. High parameter and compute costs matter in deployment.

1409.4842|Going Deeper with Convolutions (Inception)|Vision|Parallel convolutional branches capture multiple receptive-field scales. Bottleneck projections control computation. Compare branch design with a uniform sequential stack.

1608.06993|Densely Connected Convolutional Networks|Vision|Each layer receives features from preceding layers through concatenation. Feature reuse changes gradient flow and memory requirements. Concatenation is different from residual addition.

1505.04597|U-Net|Vision|An encoder-decoder network uses skip connections for precise localisation. It was developed for biomedical segmentation. Pixel-level predictions require different evaluation from image classification.

1506.02640|You Only Look Once (YOLO)|Vision|Object detection is framed as a single regression problem. Joint prediction supports fast inference. Compare localisation errors, small-object performance and throughput.

1506.01497|Faster R-CNN|Vision|A region-proposal network shares convolutional features with detection. Learned proposals replace an external proposal stage. Two-stage and one-stage detectors have different speed-quality trade-offs.

1703.06870|Mask R-CNN|Vision|An instance-mask branch extends region-based object detection. RoIAlign reduces misalignment from feature quantisation. Instance segmentation separates individual objects, not just semantic classes.

2010.11929|An Image is Worth 16x16 Words (ViT)|Vision|Image patches become tokens for a transformer encoder. Pretraining scale strongly influences performance. Compare inductive biases with convolutional networks.

2103.14030|Swin Transformer|Vision|Shifted local windows build hierarchical visual representations efficiently. Window shifts enable cross-window communication. Hierarchy supports dense prediction as well as classification.

2103.00020|Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision (CLIP)|Multimodal|Contrastive learning aligns image and text representations. Text descriptions support zero-shot classification. Performance depends on prompts, data and distribution shift.

2304.02643|Segment Anything|Multimodal|Promptable segmentation supports different user inputs through a shared model. A large data-collection process is central to the approach. Segmentation masks do not by themselves provide semantic understanding.

2301.12597|BLIP-2|Multimodal|A lightweight querying transformer bridges frozen vision and language models. Staged training aligns representations for generation. Frozen backbones reduce trainable parameters but retain inference cost.

2304.08485|Visual Instruction Tuning (LLaVA)|Multimodal|Visual features are connected to a language model and tuned with multimodal instructions. Instruction data shapes interaction behaviour. Evaluate visual grounding rather than fluency alone.

2204.14198|Flamingo|Multimodal|Gated cross-attention conditions language generation on visual inputs. Interleaved image-text examples support few-shot tasks. Visual encoding and language generation remain distinct components.

2002.05709|A Simple Framework for Contrastive Learning (SimCLR)|Representation|Augmented views of the same image form positive pairs. Contrastive training depends heavily on augmentation and batch design. Representation quality is measured through downstream evaluation.

2006.07733|Bootstrap Your Own Latent (BYOL)|Representation|An online network predicts a slowly updated target network's representations. Explicit negative pairs are not required. Architectural asymmetry and training dynamics matter for avoiding collapse.

1911.05722|Momentum Contrast (MoCo)|Representation|A queue and momentum encoder maintain a consistent dictionary for contrastive learning. This decouples dictionary size from batch size. Stale representations are an important design consideration.

2104.14294|Emerging Properties in Self-Supervised Vision Transformers (DINO)|Representation|Self-distillation learns visual features without manual labels. Teacher updates and multi-crop views guide training. Emergent attention patterns are qualitative observations, not segmentation guarantees.

2111.06377|Masked Autoencoders Are Scalable Vision Learners|Representation|A high fraction of image patches is masked and reconstructed. An asymmetric encoder-decoder reduces pretraining cost. Reconstruction targets influence learned representations.

1609.02907|Semi-Supervised Classification with Graph Convolutional Networks|Graphs|Neighbourhood aggregation combines graph structure with node features. Layer stacking propagates information over multiple hops. Oversmoothing and transductive assumptions deserve attention.

1710.10903|Graph Attention Networks|Graphs|Learned attention weights aggregate neighbouring node features. Attention is computed within graph neighbourhoods. Weights are not automatically causal explanations.

1706.02216|Inductive Representation Learning on Large Graphs (GraphSAGE)|Graphs|Neighbour sampling and aggregation learn embeddings for unseen nodes. The method supports inductive use beyond a fixed training graph. Sampling introduces a computation-variance trade-off.
